item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If the limit of existence is the physical body, then the lack-of-sensation period when that body was nonfunctional would be part of the experience of a re-animated self. If there is no mind separate from the brain, then it is solely the state of the brain that determines experiences.

Think of the mind as a camcorder. You are imagining death as turning it off. But it could just as well be that the record function keeps running, accumulating experience, but all the "lenses" inputs are disconnected. Without a reactivation like the green slime provides, there would be no difference. But once you restore full function, the first case would be a jump-skip in the recording; the second would be a long period of blank tape before the picture comes back.

…it's impossible to talk about this stuff without soundig like a pretentious douche, isn't it?

item.content:encoded: First, those last two effects are both reasonable options, and I intentionally left them as possible interpretations. Secondly, as I see it, it can still be possible that the revived is telling the truth; if 447 just brings back life to the body (since there is no soul), then it would be the same person to return to the body, since that's where "life" is kept. He knows that there's no life after death because he experienced nothing after the body died, and his death was the ultimate loss of sensation, hence oblivion in his eyes.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Cheerful existential nihilist here, and I really found myself just smiling and shaking my head here. So what if there's nothing waiting for us after death? So what if everything we do is completely pointless in the long term of the universe?

Why not try to make the world better anyway? Not for reward, not for duty, not for ambition… just for the sake of doing it. Just for the ephemeral pleasure of making another person smile.

Once you've realised that your existential angst is just as pointless as everything else, so you might as well make the best of things while you're here… to me, that's the most freeing thing I've ever thought.

I think it's funny that Scantron said that this was personally resonant "as an atheist", because as not-an-atheist, this is not only reflective of my headcanon of the Foundation but reminiscent of my general state of mind, too. Certain swathes of this monologue outline exactly how I would perceive the Foundation if it were real and really went about its business the way we present it.

I guess in that sense… I don't really find this threatening or even as deep as the well of nihilism goes. But then, "threatening" doesn't seem to be the thrust of the tale, and I appreciate it for taking a nuanced approached to a mystery that mostly invites images of mass grossness and destruction. If nothing else, it's got a nice, consistent tone. +1

item.content:encoded:
Alternative interpretation, building off of this: Experiencing nothingness is simply a facet of SCP-447. There's something after death (and the Foundation knows that because they've been there), but in the process of bringing you back, in denying you the ability to experience this afterlife, SCP-447 functionally destroys your soul and deprives a consciousness of any real meaning it could experience.

SCP-447 is bad in the same way that the Total Perspective Vortex is — plenty of things can kill your body, but SCP-447 kills your soul. And that's why its effect on dead bodies is expunged and experiments are denied — doing so would be infinitely more unethical than anything as passe as killing lots of people (because that doesn't ultimately matter), to the point where they don't want anyone to know that they've done so.

I do like the idea behind the story a lot, but I would have preferred it to be presented through a more, er, traditional storytelling technique.
